'''Daniel E. Gorenstein''' (January 1, 1923 – August 26, 1992) was an American [[mathematician]] best remembered for his contribution to the [[classification of finite simple groups]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Saxon |first=Wolfgang |date=August 28, 1992 |title=Daniel Gorenstein, Who Charted Math's Densest Fields, Dies at 69 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/08/28/nyregion/daniel-gorenstein-who-charted-math-s-densest-fields-dies-at-69.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150526065523/https://www.nytimes.com/1992/08/28/nyregion/daniel-gorenstein-who-charted-math-s-densest-fields-dies-at-69.html |archive-date=May 26, 2015 |access-date=April 27, 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

Gorenstein mastered calculus at age 12 and subsequently matriculated at [[Harvard University]],<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Dangerfield |first=Jan |title=The Math Book Big Ideas Simply Explained |last2=Davis |first2=Heather |last3=Farndon |first3=John |last4=Griffiths |first4=Jonny |last5=Jackson |first5=Tom |last6=Patel |first6=Mukul |last7=Pope |first7=Sue |last8=Parker |first8=Matt |publisher=[[DK Publishing]] |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-4654-8024-8 |location=New York |pages=319}}</ref> where he earned his bachelor's and master's degrees.<ref name=":0" /> During the Second World War, he taught mathematics to military personnel.<ref name=":1" /> After the war, he stayed at Harvard and earned his PhD 1950 under the supervision of [[Oscar Zariski]]. In his dissertation, Gorenstein introduced a duality principle for plane curves that motivated [[Alexander Grothendieck]]'s introduction of [[Gorenstein ring]]s. Gorenstein held posts at [[Clark University]] and [[Northeastern University (Boston, Massachusetts)|Northeastern University]], before moving to [[Rutgers University]] in 1969, where he remained for the rest of his life. He became the founding director of the Center for Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science ([[DIMACS]]) at Rutgers in 1989, and remained at this post until his death.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Martel |first=Michelle |title=A History of Mathematics at Rutgers |url=https://www.math.rutgers.edu/for-alumni-friends/a-history-of-mathematics-at-rutgers |access-date=April 27, 2024 |website=Department of Mathematics |publisher=Rutgers University |language=en-gb}}</ref>

He was recognized, in addition to his own research contributions such as work on [[signalizer functor]]s, as a leader in directing the classification of finite simple groups, one of the largest collaborative pieces of [[pure mathematics]] ever attempted.<ref name=":0" /> In 1972, he was a [[Guggenheim Fellow]] and a [[Fulbright Scholar]]. In 1978, he gained membership in the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. In 1989, Gorenstein won the [[Steele Prize]] in mathematical exposition from the [[American Mathematical Society]] for his book ''Finite Simple Groups: An Introduction to Their Classification'' (1982).<ref name=":0" /> In 1985, he wrote an article explaining his mathematical work to the layperson for ''[[Scientific American]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gorenstein |first=Daniel |date=1985 |title=The Enormous Theorem |url=https://academics.uccs.edu/gabrams/Math4140Fall2017/GorensteinScientificAmericanarticleDecember1985%20copy.pdf |journal=[[Scientific American]] |volume=253 |issue=6 |pages=104–115 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1285-104|url-access= |jstor=24967876}}</ref>

He died in 1992 after a brief illness. He was 69 years old.<ref name=":0" />
